segments.text: [music]
>> Hello and welcome to On the Record with
me Shereen Bhan. We're at the Infosys
headquarters here in Bengaluru and the
reason we're here is because Salil
Parekh has decided that he is going to
move on and put a successor in place. I
was here in 2018 within the very first
month that Parekh had taken over and
today, as he gets ready to exit Infosys,
he is the longest-serving CEO, a
non-founder CEO of the company. Just to
give you some numbers of what the growth
has looked like under Salil Parekh's
tenure, sales growth of 11%, profit
growth of 8%, the stock has returned 7%
and ROE of 28%. That captures the tenure
performance for Salil Parekh here at
Infosys. As he gets ready to move on
from Infosys, but perhaps also start up
all over again. Joining me now is the
man himself, Salil. Thanks very much for
joining us. It's great to have you. As I
said, life comes a full circle. I was
here in 2018 in January when you had
started your tenure and I'm here as you
have decided to transition.
Uh
but, you know, Salil,
they could have moved a special
resolution. They could have given you
more time. Did you want more time? Was
that even a conversation?
>> So, first, Shereen,
it's great to have you back here. I
think, as you just mentioned,
it was wonderful when I started, you
were here and
I think it was a bit of a war, at least
for me, given everything that was going
on in the company. Uh Uh, and today, uh
in in a very different place, I feel at
least the company is. So, thanks for
being here and thanks for doing this.
Um, I I think as you shared, the the
last several years have gone, I think,
quite well for the company. Uh, we've
grown very well, 10 billion to 20
billion.
Uh, the whole focus on digital has
helped us. Now, the AI is really well
established. We had a 8% revenue last
quarter, and we can see uh, with the
market evolution where that's going. Uh,
so, in all of that,
uh, what what I had the opportunity
here, you know, leading an iconic
institution was, uh, just an incredible
blessing. Uh, and given all of that and
the way Infosys is positioned, uh, it
looked like the right time. We have a
phenomenal team within the company. We
have leaders in the market across
delivery, across all of our functions.
Uh, so, I feel really good that this is
a great time to have that sort of
completion of my second term and have,
uh, a new person running the show now.
>> But, you know what they say, third time
is a charm, Salil. [laughter] So, you
didn't want to take that chance.
>> No, absolutely. I think, you know, all
of those things are good things, but
equally, Infosys is in a very good
place. Uh, and we've had, I think, an
incredible run going through many
different sort of global environments.
And given where we are, given where we
positioned ourselves on AI, uh, it's a
good time to make sure that we we focus
on all of the things that have happened
in the company that have supported us
for the good.
>> You know, I'll get to AI in just a
second, uh, Salil, but, uh, let let
let's walk through your wonderful campus
here. Uh, let's talk a little bit about,
uh, Ashish Dash, who, of course, comes
in to take over. October is when the
transition, in a sense, the hand-holding
will start. Uh, he will move to LA, uh,
from LA to Bengaluru. Uh,
were were there only internal candidates
that the board considered or were there
external candidates as well that the
board looked at?
>> So, the first guy is a phenomenal
leader. I've known him for many years.
We've worked together. He's a good
friend and done very well with
employees, with clients, and also with
the portfolio that he's looked at, you
know, both in terms of, you know, making
sure there's growth, making sure there's
economic returns. So, very very strong
performance. The board went through,
I think, a very good process in the way
they looked at the situation and made
all of their decisions
in in keeping in mind what we were
looking at as a company into the future.
And of course, we have an excellent set
of leaders within Infosys and
we've had this I mean, Salil himself has
been here over 30 years, but many of the
senior leaders been here for 20, 25, 30
years. So, fortunately, there's a good
set of people in the leadership
sort of domain within Infosys itself.
>> You know, Salil,
as we look forward, I also want to look
back and I also want to ask you what you
believe we should now calibrate as far
as growth expectations for the company
as well as for the industry is
concerned. And I was just looking at the
numbers to really get
an arc of what you've kind of,
you know, overseen. FY19 9% and of
course, we saw that big bump up in FY22
of almost almost 20% and then about 16%
in FY23 and then now back down to about
You know, would it be fair to assume
that we're going to now, for the
foreseeable future, be stuck in this 3
to 5% kind of range?
>> So, first, I think
what you described, if you look at the
organic growth we've had we've had
across that time from when I started the
fastest among the large companies.
What we see and and you you've seen this
industry and Infosys for years
there are cyclical sort of aspects of of
the tech spend. So, for example when
global macro GDP growth is more managed
and doing well, the growth typically on
tech is higher.
Um what we see now is really the start
of the AI expansion. If you look at
our own AI uh growth
we shared publicly, it's double-digit
quarter-on-quarter growth over the last
several quarters. So, it's a very strong
foundation. If you look at it as a
standalone at over 8% it's already a
very large part of what we are doing. A
lot of work on agents, lot of work on
modernization, lot of work with the new
coding tools.
When the other pieces of the global
environment, the macro, the GDP all
start to come together uh there'll be
more tech spend overall as well because
part of what we've seen recently is much
more attention on cost. And so, my sense
is as that cycle comes off we will start
to see good growth again. Now, of course
there's a difference when you have when
I started it was a $10 billion entity,
today we are a $20 billion entity. So,
that has its own uh sort of
uh changes in how the growth come, but I
see uh over the sort of medium longer
term horizon growth more a function of
the macro and how we execute on AI. So,
good good outlook on growth.
>> You know, Nandan has given a number of
between 300 to 400 billion is what he
expects as the addressable market, the
AI opportunity by 2030. Now, if I were
to ask you how much of that value do you
believe you can realistically capture
over the next few years?
>> So there really it's up to us how we
execute. So today what we are seeing is
for our client base, our industries,
when clients are looking at making AI
work, let's say a bank wants to build a
new KYC agent.
The the they are calling Infosys to work
with them with all of the foundation
model companies to build it for them.
And any of those processes, any of the
functions,
clients,
the Telco company wants to modernize
from an older technology to a new using
AI.
>> Right.
>> Infosys is the one they call. So we can
capture a huge amount of that. That's
really an execution play now for us
between in that $300 billion
uh
we've defined the six areas, you you may
recall, of what are the specific places
where the growth is. And now we've
started the execution and it looks
pretty good. If we continue the
execution well, which every indication
is we will, that that market share could
be quite massive.
>> You know, let me take you back to the
days of the digital transition, right? I
mean, companies like yours started
reporting digital revenue uh to the
point that you didn't need to make that
separation anymore and everything became
digital revenue.
When do you believe that's likely to
happen as far as AI is concerned? You've
just started reporting AI revenue and 8%
today as far as the company's concerned.
When do you believe you will no longer
need a separate line?
>> So there again again that that
description is exactly what we are
looking at. So as you remember,
digital we started reporting when it was
about 20% I think. And we took it over 3
4 years maybe to over 60% when it became
part of everything we were doing. So I
don't know if it's exactly the same cuz
there are indications that AI could go
faster.
>> Mhm.
>> But it also depends a little bit on the
macro because today
in AI already there's a lot of attention
on token cost.
>> Mhm.
>> So, this is move very quickly, meaning
even if you look a few months ago, there
was only discussion on can we use
the best models for everything. And
today there's already discussion on can
we use the appropriate model for any
task we're doing? And so,
within Infosys we have built something
called Topaz Fabric where we work with
15 models.
And even in each of the models we work
with the older version of that model as
well.
So, if you look at a token cost, it
for the most recent models if it's a
100, for the most efficient it's almost
five or 10 in terms of ratio. So,
all of that has to play out. When we do
that, my my sense is today we're only
looking at companies doing X, can we do
it better with agents? Tomorrow we're
going to look at
instead of X, can we do 10 X in a
company? And so, those sorts of changes
we can expand it even more massively.
So, I don't know what that horizon is,
but it's it's a transformation, it's an
execution, it's a pivot. So, the faster
we go, it could take, you know, fewer
quarters, it could take a few longer,
but the path appears fairly well laid
out.
>> You know, I I I think at the start of
the year
the nightmare for Indian IT and the big
question that was being asked is will
you be cloudified? And and and I think
from a market perspective we saw the
kind of value erosion, the wealth
erosion that took place. It's
a recovery in the last few weeks is is
still underway, of course, still
significantly lower than the kind of
peaks that companies like yours as well
as the sector have enjoyed. But, is
there now uh
uh an acknowledgement or an appreciation
that it's not all over for the Indian IT
services industry because you know you
know that the obituaries were being
written at the start of the year.
>> [laughter]
>> So my sense of me
We've always had the view that
the work we do for large companies which
is our client base requires
that as they bring in new foundation
models that we given that we know the
context what's going on the landscape in
a company that we can help and that's
seems to be getting demonstrated now so
we even internally had that view. They
were different views externally but we
seem to be seeing that coming back but
the real sort of test in my mind is as
all of that comes to bear over the next
few years but we can see the path to it
for sure. If you look at it even like
recruitment like last year we recruited
20,000 college graduates if we didn't
have that belief we wouldn't have done
that this year we already have the same
similar plan another 20,000
in the first quarter we've already done
4,000 college hires so we see you know
the the
individuals coming in from colleges
absolutely
AI native people we are training them on
our own
existing approach and then making sure
that they learn all the new tools that
we have.
We have about 80,000 people already in
the company today we're working on
coding tools for clients and and some
internal projects so
to me at least I see this as a great
opportunity for the next phase of the
transformation. Infosys my sense we will
continue to scale and grow
and and I think the sector itself, you
know, as long as we're executing to go
into AI should be okay.
>> Yeah, you know, that's the future. Let's
talk a little bit about the near term.
And I think what the market was
concerned about at the end of your
earnings and of course I don't want to
go too much into the earnings because
you've done
extensive conversations around that. But
the very sharp cut in in guidance,
especially on revenue, that has worried
people. What is it that you're seeing in
terms of the significant deterioration
in the last 3 months itself that's
forced your hand to announce such a
sharp cut?
>> So, we we changed the guidance. One of
the reasons and we shared all of this
was we had a one-time
event in terms of client change of plans
which we uh uh described. That was the
bulk of it. And then we saw which the
macro being a little bit uneven, some of
the changes in volume now. When
something like this
happens in the first quarter, it has a
flow through through the whole year. But
outside of that, if you look at our
large deals, very strong. If you look at
our margin, actually higher than what
most people were expecting. And we see a
stable sort of an outlook for margin. If
you look at free cash flow,
very strong at 950 million. So, all of
the business parameters are looking in
good shape. And then we had the the AI
which is looking strong as well. So, my
sense is
overall the business is in excellent
shape and making sure that we go through
all of the changes, whether it's with AI
which is a transformation, and with the
changes in the global environment which
is just making sure we are navigating
through that.
>> Right. Saloni, you know, I wanted to get
your comments on what we heard from
Arvind Krishna at the end of IBM's
earnings and he talked about the fact
that because there is such a priority on
infrastructure spend at this point in
time that perhaps people are holding
back on traditional IT services spends.
Are you sensing that from your clients
also?
>> So we we have seen basically our clients
much more focused on cost activities.
But we have not seen a change otherwise
in the spend. I think
a lot of clients are becoming more
sensitive on how they spend what we
discussed earlier on the token usage. So
that
is an efficiency that they are driving
through. We continue to see for example
on AI
a lot of spend which is where we getting
this sort of a growth on and and the
other piece is a little bit more
attention on cost which has been going
on more in light of the macro really for
the last few quarters
year or so. So that that is how we've
seen it without any changes.
>> Yeah, you know, competition of course
has been intense in the sector but is it
particularly intense now? I mean many of
your peers are calling out the fact that
competition is off the charts.
Somebody's breakfast is your lunch,
somebody else's dinner is your
breakfast. I mean how how
how much pressure is that putting on
margins for instance and do you expect
that to only worsen as we go forward?
>> So there again we've taken a view to be
extremely clear that we we want to make
sure that anything we do fits what our
economic profile is. So you've seen
our margin has remained resilient all
through this and actually last year it's
improved a little bit on the prior year.
Uh and we see that being part of what we
do.
The competitive intensity is is quite
quite heavy which which you described.
>> Worse than what you've seen in the last
10 years?
>> Uh
>> More intense in the last 10 years?
>> I I I've always felt it's equally
intense. So, I don't see it's increased,
but maybe there are you know, there are
different companies at different stages
of their sort of
their life cycle. So, then some people
maybe get a little bit more intense when
they're different stages.
Uh we've taken a view to make sure that
we you know, we've done
over 3.6 billion of large deals. So, we
are winning huge deals consistently.
Equally, we've been very careful on one
or two instances where the economic
outlook is definitely not fitting what
we're looking at.
>> How many of you walked away from because
economically it was not making sense for
you?
>> there you know, it's hardly
There was a discussion that we had at
the time of the results where we talked
about one specific instance in a
European client, but it's literally
nothing
which is in larger numbers. Very small.
One or two in that sense because
we are extremely competitive, but we are
also really clear that there are some
things that we want to make sure that we
manage what our economic sort of profile
of the company is. And these things
sometimes in the short run you know,
may may be sort of unusual for other
people. Other companies might see some
benefit, but we are very clear that we
want to do this in a way that makes
sense for the medium and long term.
>> You know, what I also want to understand
from you Salil, and I think this is
something that industry is grappling
with, that as you move more towards an
agentic economy, as you move more
towards agents within an organization,
what is that going to mean structurally
as far as margins are concerned? You
know,
what is the impact going to be on the
way that you price?
>> So, there there there are different
models that are already coming into
place. So, first
we have in small instances things which
look like
agents plus our own
uh software engineers sort of working on
joint teams like that.
Second,
we are looking at things where
there are business outcomes which also
become part of it. It's not all of it,
but that'll become part of it. But,
these things, at least what we've seen
in our industry and in Infosys is it
takes time to make those changes. For
the large part, it's still similar the
way the pricing works. And there's a lot
of pricing
productivity benefit which clients
themselves are seeking when they see all
the benefits that we can deliver. And
so, all that will also go on.
However, we are building these new
things which are quite
incredible if you look at some of the
agents, the work that has been going on,
some of the work we're doing with coding
tools. So, there are places where the
pricing is
let's say quite good for for the
company. There are benefits that the
clients are receiving which are quite
massive. So, both of those things are
happening now.
>> So, the benefits that the clients are
receiving on account of productivity, do
you get to leverage on that or you know
how does it work?
>> I mean, usually
there's some sharing. I think the bulk
of it still goes to the clients, but we
do get some of it because in many
instances when we bring those ideas to
clients,
they they immediately see the benefits.
So, for example, we're doing a project
on modernizing a technology environment.
So,
it will have a one-time cost which which
the client will bear and pay us, but it
will also have a huge benefit for their
running their infrastructure, their
environment ongoing which will be much
reduced. So, client will be extremely
happy in this instance, but the overall
mix they will benefit and and we will
receive some benefit.
>> You know,
how agentic will emphasis look in the
next 5 years? And what is that going to
mean as far as your workforce is
concerned going forward? You're hiring
today as you pointed out last year,
20,000 fresh graduates, but as we move
more into this agentic future, what will
it realistically mean both in terms of
hiring as well as in terms of workflow?
>> So, the work is you know, it's like uh
today's foundation models that exist are
like a very
uh great efficiency tool that an
engineer can use, a software engineer
can use. So, for them
they're doing different things by using
these tools. It's a like an advanced
toolkit that you have with you. So, my
sense and this is evolving, so it's not
like we've reached an asymptote or
anything in the foundation model
technology yet. So, my sense is that
evolution will keep enhancing. So, the
people who learn, which is our
reskilling or the new graduates who
learn these technologies well, will be
more the beneficiaries.
>> Mhm.
>> They'll be really native AI people as
you know, as years go on in the next
year, 2 years, 5 years. And that will be
the type of person that works you know,
we have a plan to
sort of have 6,000 frontier engineers.
We'll have and this is over the next few
years, but over 5, 7 years we'll have
more and more of that sort of capability
within the company that can work with
clients. So, my sense is they'll be
absolutely sort of AI native type of
people who are working there.
>> So, these frontier engineers, would
would this be the same as FDEs
or or is this is this a is this a
different league altogether?
>> No, so I I mean, there's some people are
using that terminology
uh FDs. What we are doing with frontier
engineers is in many ways making sure
that people who understand the
technology
but who also understand the engineering
of it. Meaning, how does it work in a
company and then understand the
business. So,
that's the skill that that frontier
engineer has
uh and we already have a good good team
internally. We are making sure that
people go through internal assessments
so that we we can be certain this is
frontier engineer who can work with
clients. And then we are also scaling up
from outside.
>> You know, Salil and I think this is not
just a criticism of of any one company
individually, but it's a collective sort
of criticism of the Indian IT services
industry that
could you have done more as far as IP
and innovation is concerned? Could you
have used and deployed your capital more
on R&D and innovation as opposed to
buybacks and and dividends? How do you
today, from your vantage point,
realistically respond to that criticism?
How valid is that?
>> So, if you look at Infosys, I think
our approach, you know, essentially we
are a services company which works
across the landscape of all the new
technologies.
With that being said,
we have already built two small language
models.
Building large language models is a
different
economic approach and
it's it's very different from what we do
within a services business. But the
small language models that we built
are very clear. For example, we have one
for banking. This uses fewer parameters.
It builds on data sets which are
non-client based but that we have an
understanding of. And with that trained
model, we are already creating massive
impact within in this case the banking
banking client base. And then we build a
small language model, which is across IT
operations, which is a little bit more
horizontal, and that's working well as
well. So, our
approach is given the sort of
tech services business that we have,
we have made sure that we do what is
appropriate for that business to scale
up
and work with all the different models.
If you look at today,
you know, working with 15 models, there
are different models that are good for
different things, and we bring that
expertise or knowledge into our clients,
which is where the real value of Infosys
is to make sure that's easily available
for all of those clients.
>> You know, so the current debate on
globally at this point in time,
open-source, open weights, the limits to
renting intelligence, uh you know, Satya
Nadella actually saying that look, every
company will need to have its own model.
As you look at the AI future and the
conversations that are happening
globally and what would be important and
imperative for Indian IT services
companies like yours, what do you
believe where do you believe the
challenge lies, but more importantly,
what will you prioritize?
>> So, there I think first
we we work with 15 models, some of them
are open weight, some of them are
closed.
We work with different versions, meaning
older models, newer models.
What is critical in all of this debate,
at least from our view, is
clients should have the ability to
ensure that they manage their data, but
also have control over
what is distinctive about their
business, which they should be careful
doesn't
leave their sort of ecosystem without
their knowledge or control.
>> Mhm.
>> Uh and that all models have the ability
to provide that in different ways. Open
way, it's very clear. But other models
will also do that because
not no large company wants to leave
their own sovereign sort of knowledge
that not just the data which can become
outside the company.
So, what we have done by building
sort of Topaz fabric is make that more
possible for our clients.
>> Mhm.
>> And the earlier discussion on token
efficiency, those are two important
elements today which is you know, I
don't want to lose what's differentiated
for me as a company and I want to do it
in a way that's efficient. Uh and that
is the more critical debate at least as
we see it for large companies.
Uh others, I think of course, you know,
there are big global players on tech or
on the labs. Each of them have their own
perspective on what they're driving and
each of them have their own objectives
also. But this is how we are looking at
it and we are working with each of them.
Uh
m- many of them have all the
ingredients. It's a question of making
it sort of let's say ready for clients.
And in that way, what we build with
fabric helps our clients do it a little
bit more easily. Many clients are doing
it themselves as well. So, it's not like
you know, once you have a sense of what
this is, it's not that difficult to put
it in place so you don't lose it.
>> That's the fear. Many clients are now
doing it themselves and which is the
question that people are asking that
will it not start to impact your ability
to work with clients as they build that
in-house capability?
>> It's not the capability. What I mean is
they're doing it themselves in
understanding what this implication is.
At the end, we have the scale and the
experience across 1,800 different
clients. So, large companies that work
with us want to take the benefit or
advantage of that.
>> Not log you out.
>> At least at this stage we are seeing
tremendous growth on the AI services
side. But this
realization that these things are also
critical is what I mean in terms of the
clients are starting to see. If you look
back, you know, a few months, maybe a
year, there was a little bit of let's
just get something going with AI, which
is now changed to let's do it in a way
that makes
sense for the for our company. And which
is where I think we we, you know, we can
play a huge role in that.
>> You know, you've been fairly acquisitive
in your tenure, Salil, but do you
believe that the way that you do M&A,
the kinds of targets that you go after
will need to change given the AI future
that we're all entering?
>> The I think the targets will evolve
because we've done a lot of acquisitions
on industry or capability. So, in AI
today it'll be a little bit more focused
on capability, but there's not that many
companies of even decent scale. They're
they're much smaller.
But the approach, which is a little bit
of discipline on what we will pay for
it,
how will it integrate, how is the
culture of that company, will that work?
>> Is this a buyer's market? Is it a
seller's market today?
>> Well, AI companies, I think not so many,
so they they have a great advantage if
they build a good business. My my guess
is many people will look to acquire
them.
>> You know, you talked about
differentiation. I want to understand
from you some of your peers are getting
into the data center business. Some of
them are actually picking up equity
stakes in AI companies, HCL Tech with
with Sarvam, TCS doing data centers as
well. Is that something that you foresee
for Infosys?
>> So, we've looked at that and we are not
planning to do a go into the data center
business. So, we've looked at
from our perspective, our balance sheet,
the potential needs of cash to build out
any scale data center,
and then other requirements, you know,
which are around essentially uh,
projects around energy, uh, and it's
something that we have decided at this
stage, uh, is not something we will
benefit from, uh, especially given, uh,
our balance sheet, uh, because some of
the cash needs could be quite, quite
massive. So, we've looked at it uh, from
the management team, we've looked at it
uh, in our board, and we've decided not
to do it.
>> Not to go to the data center route, but
uh, AI, and I put this in the context
of, uh, you know, what what has been the
big headline, should Infosys have bet on
OpenAI when that was, uh, the option in
2014, it would have been a
entirely different story today. Uh, you
know, as as you look back at that, do
you believe that that was a big missed
opportunity?
>> Well, I think in many ways,
>> I mean, you were not there then, but
from an outsider's perspective, and now
as an insider, do you believe that that
was a missed opportunity?
>> Well, I think we've we built
partnerships with
AI labs all through, uh, even earlier
on, there were discussions with
